analysis.one_liner: Caps the nation's greenhouse gas emissions through a shrinking pool of tradeable pollution allowances.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 11 cosponsors, including 4 Republicans, but never left the Senate committee; its only action after referral was a subcommittee hearing in July 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set a declining national limit on greenhouse gas emissions, requiring power plants, factories, and petroleum refiners to hold one allowance for every ton they emit, with companies free to buy, sell, bank, or borrow allowances. A new Climate Change Credit Corporation would manage allowances and use trading proceeds to reduce consumer costs, help displaced workers, and fund adaptation for low-income people. The bill also pours federal loan guarantees into nuclear, clean coal, solar, and biofuel projects and funds a broad climate technology research agenda.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary Americans exposed to climate change harm, through a mandated declining emissions cap, plus consumers, who would receive trading proceeds as rebates or cost reductions with preferential treatment for those least able to pay, and dislocated workers eligible for transition assistance.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The public and low-income energy consumers

how_it_helps.text: Beginning in 2012, covered electric, industrial, and commercial entities and petroleum refiners must submit one tradeable allowance for each metric ton of greenhouse gases emitted, under a cap that declines from 6,130 million metric tons to 2,096 million metric tons for years after 2049.

The Climate Change Credit Corporation must use trading proceeds to reduce costs borne by consumers, with preferential treatment for those who can least afford increased costs, and to fund transition assistance for dislocated workers and communities and adaptation programs for low-income populations.
The bill creates a national greenhouse gas database with public, verifiable emissions reporting and penalties of three times the market value of missing allowances for noncompliance.

analysis.who_pays: Covered utilities, industrial emitters, and petroleum refiners, who must obtain allowances or cut emissions and are expected to pass some costs to customers in energy and fuel prices; taxpayers also back any defaults on the bill's full-faith-and-credit clean energy loan guarantees.
analysis.who_pays_short: Power plants, refiners, industrial emitters, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Most allowances would be allocated to covered entities without cost under the allocation process, so the bill gives major emitters valuable permits rather than charging them, while still allowing compliance costs to be passed through to customers.

Covered entities can satisfy up to 30 percent of their requirement with offsets, international credits, and sequestration projects, and can borrow up to 25 percent of a year's allowance requirement, giving emitters room to delay real emissions cuts.

The clean energy financing title directs federal loans of up to 80 percent of project costs to nuclear reactors, coal gasification plants, biofuel facilities, and solar projects, backed by the full faith and credit of the United States, putting taxpayers at risk if projects fail.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have imposed the first binding national limit on greenhouse gas emissions with real penalties and a declining cap, a substantial public benefit, and it directs trading proceeds toward consumers and low-income households. But it is not cost-free: the biggest emitters would receive allowances free of charge, offset and borrowing flexibility would let some emissions cuts slip years into the future, and the loan guarantee program puts taxpayer money behind first-of-a-kind nuclear and coal projects. The design leans toward easing industry's transition as much as protecting the public, but the cap and penalties are real.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, a subcommittee held one hearing in July 2007, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 12, 2007 by Senator Lieberman with Senators McCain, Lincoln, Snowe, Obama, Collins, and Durbin as original cosponsors, and was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.
It gathered 11 cosponsors, 4 Republicans and 7 Democrats.
The committee's Subcommittee on Private Sector and Consumer Solutions to Global Warming and Wildlife Protection held hearings on July 24, 2007.
No further action was taken on the bill for the remainder of the 110th Congress, which ended January 3, 2009; it never received a committee vote or a Senate floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The utilities, petroleum refiners, and industrial emitters the bill would have regulated were better off, since no mandatory national emissions cap took effect, and no one gained the consumer rebates, worker transition aid, or emissions reductions the bill promised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulated energy emitters avoided a mandatory cap

for.name: 11 cosponsors (7 Democrats, 4 Republicans)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral for the rest of the Congress; its subcommittee held one hearing and the committee never voted on it, keeping it off the Senate floor.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory national limits on greenhouse gas emissions throughout this period, and climate cap-and-trade bills faced a veto threat from his administration.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan, with 7 Democratic and 4 Republican cosponsors including Republicans McCain, Snowe, and Collins, but no votes were ever taken so no party split on the merits is recorded.

industries.note: The bill caps their emissions but allocates tradeable allowances to covered entities at no cost, handing major emitters valuable permits and locking in their role as the gatekeepers of the emissions market. Their compliance costs would largely flow to customers through energy prices.

The bill authorizes federal loans covering up to 80 percent of project costs for the first advanced reactor designs, funds nuclear fuel cycle research, and creates a program to reduce first-time licensing costs for new reactor designs. Nuclear expansion also serves the bill's decarbonization goal, so its gain runs alongside the public's interest in lower emissions.

The emission cap directly penalizes conventional coal combustion, the largest source of covered emissions, but the bill subsidizes up to three integrated gasification combined cycle coal plants with carbon capture through federal loans of up to 80 percent of project costs. Coal's interest in avoiding any cap runs against the public's, while the subsidies for capture technology pull the other way.

Refiners must submit one allowance for every ton of greenhouse gases their transportation fuels will emit when burned, a direct new cost on their core product. That cost is the mechanism the bill uses to curb emissions the public wants reduced, though refiners would pass much of it to drivers.

The bill provides federal financing for up to three large-scale solar facilities and three large-scale cellulosic biofuel plants, funded by auction proceeds from allowances. These industries' growth supports the bill's emissions goals.

The bill creates a market for tradeable allowances that can be sold, exchanged, purchased, banked, and borrowed, generating a new commodity and trading business. Its value to the public depends on how well the market is policed against manipulation.
